title: array_find(), array_find_key(), array_any() and array_all()
summary: PHP 8.4 added four short-circuiting array-search functions: array_find(), array_find_key(), array_any() and array_all().
new_code_policy: On a feature ceiling of 8.4 or above, prefer array_find()/array_find_key() over a hand-written foreach-with-break when searching for the first matching element or key, and prefer array_any()/array_all() over an array_filter()-plus-count() or manual-loop predicate check.
existing_code_policy: Once the project's PHP floor reaches 8.4, existing foreach-with-break searches and array_filter()-plus-count()/count()-comparison predicate checks over a plain callback can be replaced incrementally with the matching new function; verify the callback has no side effects relied upon for elements past the first match, since the new functions short-circuit and array_filter() does not.
guideline: Use array_find() / array_find_key() to locate the first matching element or key, and array_any() / array_all() to test a predicate across an array, instead of a manual foreach loop or an array_filter()-based workaround.
details: PHP 8.4 added four functions to the Standard extension (RFC array_find): array_find($array, $callback) returns the first element for which $callback returns true, or null if none match; array_find_key($array, $callback) returns the first matching key, or null; array_any($array, $callback) returns true as soon as one element satisfies $callback; array_all($array, $callback) returns true only if every element satisfies $callback. All four short-circuit: they stop iterating at the first element that decides the result, unlike array_filter(), which always evaluates every element and returns an array of matches that then has to be measured or indexed into. $callback receives (value, key) in that order for all four functions.
notes: All four functions short-circuit on the deciding element instead of evaluating the whole array, which is the main behavioral advantage over an array_filter()-based workaround and the reason a callback with side effects meant to run over every element must not be migrated blindly.

array_find() and array_find_key() return null when nothing matches, so callers searching for a value that can itself legitimately be null need an explicit array_find_key() !== null check rather than testing the found value for null.
